title: Can See Through Your Bills but Can't Touch Your Money: Claude Enters Personal Finance
excerpt: Anthropic announced it is adding personal finance capabilities to Claude, beginning this week as a gradual rollout in the United States to Pro, Max, and Ultra s
content_html:
Anthropic announced it is adding personal finance capabilities to Claude, beginning this week as a gradual rollout in the United States to Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers. After linking their bank cards, users can simply ask questions in natural language, pulling a full view of accounts scattered across different places into the conversation all at once, without having to open each banking app one by one and do the math themselves. For individual users, this means gaining a financial helper that is always on call and charges no consulting fee.

But Anthropic has kept the permissions tightly locked down: the feature is read-only, so it cannot transfer or manage funds, nor invest on your behalf. At the same time, the finance section carries no ads and does not push sponsorships, and Claude itself does not issue credit cards, make loans, or operate its own savings accounts, ensuring its answers remain objective and direct.

Getting answers to "Where did the money go?" In practice, Claude feels more like a household accountant who never gets annoyed: it can pull up balances and individual transactions, and explain unfamiliar terms. When there are still 10 days until payday at the end of the month, ask "Where did all my money go this month?" and it will summarize all linked accounts and break down the spending by category. Ask as a follow-up whether there are any unusual charges, and it will go through every account, helping users catch duplicate charges, unexplained fees, and even subscriptions that have quietly increased in price all year.

It can also field more macro-level questions—"Are my expenses exceeding my income?" or "What is APR, and how much extra interest has it cost me this year?" Claude will first explain the terminology clearly, then calculate the total interest. Users can also have it generate weekly spending charts, a calendar of upcoming bills, or custom dashboards—and revise them at any time.

It can help, but investment advice is off the table Anthropic repeatedly stresses that the personal finance feature is only meant to help you understand your own money and does not provide investment advice. It also admits that results may be wrong, so it encourages users to ask for the transaction details behind the data and, when important amounts are involved, to verify them with their bank. At a time when AI is rushing into financial use cases, this restraint of "only diagnosing, never prescribing" is perhaps its most striking selling point—after all, between understanding your bills and managing your money for you lies an insurmountable red line of trust.
